One team handles the design, the planning, the building regulations and the build, so you deal with the same people from the first visit to the finished room.

It takes knowing how the rules work.

planning.title: Planning permission for an extension in Sevenoaks
paragraphs: This is where Sevenoaks is different, so it is worth understanding before you fall in love with a design.

Your planning authority is Sevenoaks District Council. Around 93 per cent of the district is Metropolitan Green Belt, more than 60 per cent sits within the Kent Downs National Landscape to the north or the High Weald National Landscape to the south, and there are 41 conservation areas. Very few homes here sit outside all of those.
In plain terms, three things follow:

In the Green Belt, you can still extend, but scale matters. An extension is usually acceptable as long as it is not a disproportionate addition to the original house. As a rule of thumb the council has treated additions beyond roughly half the original floor area as disproportionate, though every case is judged on its own merits.

Permitted development is reduced in the protected areas. Many houses keep some permitted development rights even in the Green Belt, but those rights are cut back in the National Landscapes and conservation areas, which between them cover much of the district. Design and materials are held to a higher standard.
Listed buildings need separate consent, and Sevenoaks has a great many of them.

None of this means you cannot get a good extension built. It means the design has to be right first time and the application has to be handled properly. We work out exactly where your property stands before you commit to anything, and we prepare and manage the application for you. Even where an extension is permitted development, almost all still need building regulations approval, which we also handle.
Building on Sevenoaks' greensand ridge
The ground here is as varied as the planning, and it changes what your foundations need to do.

Sevenoaks sits on the Greensand Ridge, a band of sandy stone that runs east to west through west Kent. It gives the town its high ground and its views, which also means many plots slope. The greensand is firm in places and softer in others, and where it meets the clay beneath, springs and damp ground can appear along the base of the ridge. To the south the ground turns to heavy Gault and Weald clay, which shrinks and swells with the seasons and moves most near mature trees.

A sloping site, a spring line or a change from sand to clay all affect how an extension is founded, and on some plots that means a ground investigation before work starts. We plan the groundwork around the site you actually have rather than assuming it is flat and uniform.

cost.title: What an extension costs in Sevenoaks
paragraphs: Cost comes down to size, specification, ground conditions and finish, and Sevenoaks adds a couple of local factors.

Protected settings often call for higher quality materials and more design work, and sloping or spring line plots can mean more groundwork. As a general guide for this part of the South East, single storey extensions commonly run at a few thousand pounds per square metre of finished space, with double storey often better value per square metre. Treat those figures as a starting point, not a quote.

faqs.q: Can I extend my house in Sevenoaks if it is in the Green Belt?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The Green Belt does not ban extensions, it limits their scale. As long as the work is not a disproportionate addition to the original house, it can normally go ahead. As a guide the council has treated additions beyond roughly half the original floor area as disproportionate, but each case is judged on its own merits, and we assess yours before you plan anything.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission for an extension in Sevenoaks?
faqs.a: It depends on your property. The Kent Downs and High Weald National Landscapes and the district's conservation areas reduce permitted development rights, and the Green Belt limits scale, so more projects here need permission than in most areas. We check exactly where you stand with Sevenoaks District Council and handle any application for you.

faqs.q: How do I get a quote for my extension?
faqs.a: Call us on 07920 731533 or send the enquiry form on this page. We arrange a free, no-obligation site visit, look at your home, plot and the planning position, and give you a clear, itemised written quote for the actual project.

faqs.q: Is the first visit really free and no-obligation?
faqs.a: Yes. The visit and the quote are free, and there is no pressure to go ahead. If the timing or the numbers are not right for you, that is completely fine.

faqs.q: Do you work on period, listed and high-value homes?
faqs.a: Yes. Sevenoaks has a lot of period, ragstone, timber framed and listed property, and we extend and renovate it sympathetically, working with architects where needed and handling listed building consent where it applies.

faqs.q: Why does Sevenoaks' ground matter for my foundations?
faqs.a: The town sits on a greensand ridge, so plots often slope, the ground can vary from firm to soft, and springs can appear where the greensand meets the clay below. Heavy clay lies to the south. All of this affects how an extension is founded, so we check the ground before we start.

faqs.q: Which areas around Sevenoaks do you cover?
faqs.a: Sevenoaks town and the surrounding villages, including Riverhead, Dunton Green, Otford, Kemsing, Seal, Sevenoaks Weald and Westerham, plus the wider county. Call us and we will confirm your postcode.
